Research and Creative Activities Committee and SubCommittee Reports – Chair Meenach presented the annual committee report which outlined the charge and fundamental tasks of the committee for the academic year.
She noted that ordinary endeavors like setting research priorities and supporting research faculty shifted mid-year as the committee sought ways to support personnel affected by the spate of Federal Executive Orders that resulted in a halt to the flow of F&A funds.
She then addressed the following in detail: i.
FY ‘24 Overhead Report - The Committee for Review of the Distribution of Facilities and Administrative (Overhead) Funds is chaired by the Chair of the Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA).
Chair Meenach explained the committee structure and noted that the group had advanced several significant recommendations that she hopes will be enacted in the near future.

There seems to be a need to restructure the committee in a big-picture way.
There is also a need for an overhead funds “best practices guide” that would set the stage for more uniform policies and practices across colleges and guarantee more uniform approaches to distribution and utilization of F&A funds.

Overview.
There is renewed interest in ocean acoustics due to undersea defense applications as well as concerns about the effects of anthropogenic noise (e.g., from offshore wind farms) on marine animals.
The US Navy recently began a five-year, $2.4 billion investment in industrial base and workforce development support, including nearly $750 million in FY23 for the submarine industrial base.
In the realm of offshore renewable energy, the US has a goal of installing 30 gigawatts of offshore wind farms by 2030, or enough to power more than 10 million homes for a year.
One of the major objectives of the graduate certificate is to provide an option for students from engineering, oceanography, or other fields who would like to have graduate preparation in ocean acoustics.
Many of the courses below are already offered in a hybrid mode indicated by the asterisks.
We propose that an adequate number of hybrid courses be available for this certificate.
A concern for the public and environmentalists is the ocean noise impact of wind farm construction on marine mammals and fish.
Both the defense and offshore wind industries need people with expertise in ocean acoustics.

URI is uniquely qualified to deliver this graduate certificate in ocean acoustics to meet the knowledge needs of these workforces.
URI's mission includes a commitment to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
This graduate certificate in underwater acoustics will support that mission by educating engineers, oceanographers, marine biologists, and others in the important aspects of sound in the ocean.

MINUTES
FACULTY SENATE MEETING
Thursday, April 16, 2026
3:00 p.m. - 5:00 p.m. In Person
Hope Room - Higgins Welcome Center
Remote option via ZOOM
1. Call to order of the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty meeting by President Parlange at 3:02 pm.
2. Call to order of the Faculty Senate Meeting immediately following the General Faculty - Graduate Faculty Meeting by Faculty Senate President Williams. All Senators were on hand except Senators Burns, Deng, Ghonem, Liu, Lundy, Martin, Matson, Porto,Thomas, Zhang, and Yuan (sabbatical). Ex officio members and others in attendance included: President Parlange, Vice Provost Adams, Vice Provost Johnson, VP’s Reynolds, Jenkins, Benson, Mello, Associate VP’s Libutti and Lavan, Deans Dennis, VanderGheynst, Meyerand, LaPlante, and DeBoef, Past President Walls, and RFA Representative Honhart.

a. SPECIAL REMEMBRANCE of Faculty Member, Faculty Senator, and General Education Committee Chair Kathy Quick - Faculty Senate President Travis Williams paid tribute to former GEC Chair and A&S faculty member Kathy Quick, and he read a statement from her Department of Art and Art History colleagues who could not be present. The statements emphasized the jolt and collective sorrow experienced by the community with the loss of a colleague in the prime of their career. Chair Quick’s strong work ethic, willingness to serve and to lead, and her thoughtfulness and good nature will be missed by all, students, faculty, and staff alike.
3. REPORT OF THE UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT/OTHER ADMINISTRATORS

1. Updates and Announcements - President Parlange thanked all faculty who participated in URI Day at the Statehouse, as well as other recent events, like World Quantum Day. Faculty were reminded that Budget Model Town Halls are ongoing in the Colleges, and other notable events, like the Excellence Awards and the annual Day of Giving, are also coming up this month. The spring commencement ceremonies are set for May 15 - 17 and all faculty are strongly encouraged to participate. President Parlange provided a brief update on the proposed Medical School, noting the initiative has moved into ‘Phase 2 of exploration,’ which involves detailed financial feasibility investigations, analysis of existing gaps in service provision and training pipelines, and other studies and assessments. He also provided a brief update on his and VP Abby Benson’s efforts to ‘undo’ the state-imposed cap on FTE’s at URI, which has been in place for far too long.
2. Administrative Report on UM Chapter 5 - amends Sec. 5.41.11 to update the Space Allocation Committee for alignment with current practice - The report was tabled pending possible revisions.

3. Report on results of College of Education Dean Dennis’ evaluation, consistent with Chapter 10 of the University Manual. (Sec. 10.90.15) A point of order was raised about the senate’s authority to hear the report but it was overruled. Vice Provost Adams, filling in for Provost Wolfe, provided a summary of the evaluation, noting results were generally favorable across all metrics.
4. Presidential Administrative Report on Chapter 2 with related additions to Chapter 9 of the University Manual. Vice Provost Adams presented the report, noting it had been introduced and discussed at the January 22, 2026 meeting. The legislation was moved, seconded, and approved.
5. Status of Actions Forwarded to the President:
* The following Bills were signed by President Parlange on 3/18/26
* Curriculum & Standards Committee Bill #25-26-6B
* Graduate Council (GC) Bill #25-26-5B
* FSEC Bills #25-26-10 and#25-26-11
* Administrator Bill #25-26-02
* CASC Bill #25-26-6C and GC Bill #25-26-5C, which require final approval by the Board of Trustees.
4. REPORTS OF OFFICERS AND THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE
1. Announcements - Faculty Senate President Williams

i. Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Pharmacy - Thank you Dean LaPlante!
ii. Call for Nominations: At the October Faculty Senate meeting, Sens. Kendall Moore, William Krieger, and Alison Roberts were chosen as this year’s Nominating Committee. Per Section 5.2 of the Senate By-Laws, the Nominating Committee shall prepare a slate of candidates for one (1) one-year and two (2) two-year vacancies on the Executive Committee. The Executive Committee Election shall be held May 7, 2026. Please reach out to a member of the Nominating Committee if you are interested in this role.

iii. Announcement regarding making rooms available to rent to grad students - VP Preisser offered a reminder about concerns recently shared by the Graduate Student Association related to the temporary closure of Graduate Village. Dozens of students remain on a waitlist for housing. In an effort to ensure that all enrolled students have access to appropriate housing, FSEC encourages faculty and staff, especially those who live in close proximity to campus, to consider offering a room to rent. VP Preisser encouraged faculty to spread the word, and suggested that they explore relevant housing webpages or reach out to him directly for more information.

iv. ‘All-hands’ curriculum meeting prior to the start of fall semester 2026 - VP Preisser announced that the Faculty Senate and Vice Provost Adams are co-hosting a mandatory meeting on September 1, at 1 pm, aimed at improving curriculum proposal quality and review process consistency in Kuali. The meeting would be required for Deans and Associate Deans who have approval roles in the CMS and it is strongly recommended that the faculty chairs of college-level curriculum committees also attend. More information will be forthcoming but affected parties need to make sure this meeting is in their calendars.
2. Disposition of the Minutes - Faculty Senate President Williams
i. Minutes of the Faculty Senate Meeting of 3/12/26 were approved.
3. Activities of the Executive Committee - Senate Vice President Preisser noted the important work of FSEC reflected in the following minutes. There were no questions.
i. Executive Committee Meetings of March 6, March 13, and March 27, 2026 meetings. (No meeting on 3/20 due to Spring Break.)
d. Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee: FSEC recommends the following bills:

i. Approval of Faculty Senate Meeting Calendar for AY 2026-2027. Pres. Williams noted that FSEC has recommended a meeting calendar that prioritizes ‘third Thursdays’ for consistency, while avoiding holidays, breaks, and cultural or religious celebrations that preclude work. The calendar was approved.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26 And 3/12/26 meetings. Pres. Williams noted the proposal had been discussed by the faculty senate at previous meetings and is now offered for approval. It was moved to the senate docket for action by FSEC and was seconded. Questions were raised from the floor about some particulars of the bill and FSEC members responded. Comments were also offered from the floor noting one senator’s outstanding concerns about the bill as written. A motion was made to table the bill in its entirety. Pres. Williams noted a motion to table is not debatable or amendable and requires a ⅔ majority for approval. The motion to table passed.
iii. Ratification of appointment to the Space Allocation Committee: Leon Thiem, representing the College of Engineering. A motion to ratify was approved.

iv. FSEC Bill 2025-2026-12 regarding precluding use of the Veteran’s Day holiday as an instructional day - VP Preisser noted that while State and Federal calendars list Veteran’s Day as a holiday, language in the University Manual does not preclude its use as an instructional day. FSEC sought to clear up any confusion via the proposed amendment, which was moved for action by FSEC and seconded from the floor. College of Education senators inquired whether or not the current proposal was the result of their petition last month to amend the University Manual to preclude the use of Indigenous People’sDay/Columbus (IP/C) Day as an instructional day. VP Preisser answered affirmatively, explaining that the detailed review of UM Sec. 8.70.25 that occurred with their proposal marked the first time the ACC, CBUM and FSEC had all taken an in-depth look at the relevant language in quite some time, and the question of Veteran’s Day seemed to warrant clarification independent of what happens with the IP/C Day legislation, which is still under consideration. In response to further questions, VP Preisser confirmed that approval of the subject bill does not preclude approval of the IP/C Day bill, but he acknowledged that the constrained number of available instructional days in certain fall semesters certainly makes the Calendar Committee’s work more challenging.

5. SPECIAL REPORTS:
1. Bill 2025-2026-Joint-01, a joint proposal of the University Administration, FSEC, and the SCLC regarding reorganization of the Office of the University Ombuds. Faculty Senate President Williams explained that the proposal was the result of work done by multiple committees and individuals over the course of more than a year. Also, the plan to professionalize the Office of the Ombuds had been discussed at previous senate meetings, including, most recently, the March 12 meeting. With no further questions or discussion, there was a motion and second to approve the proposal. The motion was approved.
2. Student Senate Resolution on Accessible Education Material, as approved by the Student Senate on March 25, 2026. Tabled.

3. Kuali pause for proposal submissions, summer 2026 - Faculty Senate Specialist Spitale, FSEC member Trimm, and Enrollment Services Assoc. Director Humphrey. Specialist Spitale explained that a pause in new Kuali submissions is planned for the summer months to allow system administrators the opportunity to make much-needed updates to workflows and user experience features. All proposals entered by 5/15 will still advance through the approval process to the Dean-level of review. Any proposal not approved by the relevant dean by 6/1 will revert to draft form. Such drafts will remain in the system and will still be viewable, but will need to be resubmitted at a later date to advance toward approval. Normal proposal submission procedures and workflows will resume on 8/15. Additional information is available via the Curriculum Toolkit on the Faculty Senate’s webpage. Questions from the floor were offered, including inquiries about the degree to which suggestions from the various college curriculum committees factor into the update. It was noted that the current effort is focused more on compliance with the curricular streamlining initiative approved by the faculty senate earlier this year, but it is hoped that this year’s initiative will lay the groundwork for future short pauses wherein incremental process improvements like those that would be suggested by the curriculum committees might be made.

6. REPORTS OF STANDING AND SPECIAL COMMITTEES
a. Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Furong Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering one new temporary course and fifteen new permanent courses, as well as numerous course modifications across five colleges.
ii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07B, Programs, covering multiple program modifications, including to specializations and minors, in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Engineering, Health Sciences, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
iii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07C, covering two new programs, one in the College of Arts and Sciences and one in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
b. Curricular Reports from the Graduate Council to the Faculty Senate - The following bills were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.

i. Bill 2025-2026-06A, Courses, covering multiple course modifications across seven colleges, along with several new courses in the the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Education, Engineering, Pharmacy, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-06B, Programs, including several program modifications, along with new certificates and specializations.
c. Centers and Institutes Review Committee - Chair Porto - The CIRC is required to present annually on any new Centers and Institutes and on the rechartering status of other C/I’s reviewed. Tabled to the May 7 meeting.

d. Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee Annual Report- Chair Romanow praised her fellow committee members and noted they have had a very busy and productive year. The TAAC was involved in the review and approval of several key pieces of legislation this year, including the creation of a President’s List and modernizing the Second Grade Option. They were also involved in the curricular streamlining initiative and the reconfiguration of the Honors Program. As a result of legislation approved last year, the Committee now has a role to play in Admissions and is still determining, with AVP Libutti’s help, how that new charge will be implemented. In terms of future priorities, the Committee has been tasked with looking at UM provisions related to academic dishonesty, especially where it intersects with grade disputes. The Committee hopes to craft relevant amendments for consideration next year.

e.
Budget and Administration Committee Annual Report - Chair Triki explained that his committee’s primary task this year has been to try to measure faculty sentiment toward the new budget mode via a survey distributed broadly to the community.
As of now, the Committee intends, according to Chair Triki, to share their results with the Financial Strategy and Planning Office so that a conversation about improving messaging might be had.
It has not yet been decided how the data collected might otherwise be shared or disseminated.
Based on the survey results, the Committee had concluded that there seems to be a serious disconnect between the actual outcomes of the budget model roll-out and the faculty’s perception of those outcomes.
As examples, a majority of those surveyed did not see the new model as improving transparency or ensuring a more fair allocation of resources across colleges.
Chair Triki suggested that expanding dissemination of information about the details and mechanics of the budget might result in more positive perceptions.
VP Jenkins asked if current sentiment around higher education generally might have colored the survey results.

She enumerated several recent and ongoing concerns and challenges facing universities around the country (constrained research funding, various Federal actions, outside influence and interference in curricular matters, etc.) and suggested that the current landscape likely has a negative ‘baseline mood’ undercurrent that would be hard to measure.
Chair Triki agreed that the survey probably did roll out at an unfortunate time for measuring faculty understanding and satisfaction.
He noted that one positive takeaway from the results was the degree to which faculty are engaged and paying attention, and he praised their resilience in the face of unrelenting bad news.

f. Committee on Technology and Infrastructure Annual Report - Chair Wallace noted the many projects his committee tackled this year, including providing input to improve Brightspace and EdTech operations, helping to recreate a searchable classroom database, and suggesting strategies for improving the IT contracts/software approval process. They also provided important outreach to faculty about their roles in website editing, and helped raise awareness about current IT Policies. Priorities for next year will include understanding faculty needs and habits around responsible AI use in research, and aiding in Brightspace file recovery and migration, among other things.
7. CALL for NEW BUSINESS - None.
8. ADJOURNMENT - The meeting adjourned at 4:35 pm.

Considering the Honors Contract as an Effective Tool for Furthering Honors Education at URI SUMMARY This document briefly explores the concept of honors contracts, formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, uniting students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an hon- ors level through additional work tailored to the “broader, deeper and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC).
Contracts are recog- nized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
Successful honors contracts depend on effective setup, management, and assessment at the hon- ors administration level.
Customization to students’ and faculty interests is essential, providing personalized educational journeys and one-on-one time with instructors.
Students looking to set up contracts should follow a structured approach, guided by honors administration.

This could include early communication about opportunities, advising to educate students on the process and benefits, and encouraging them to approach advisors when identify- ing contract possibilities.
Initiating the process involves engaging with faculty, guided by advis- ing, before registration.
Detailed contracts specifying the project, its outcomes, deadlines, and contact schedules, ensure clarity.
Faculty handle grading, with the honors organization approving credits.
Contracts should bridge the gap between honors and non-honors classrooms, maintaining high standards and clear expectations.
To ensure the effectiveness of honors contracts, too routine or casual use must be prevented.
They should complement, not replace, the program’s curriculum, while preserving community and support.
Faculty involvement should be incentivized and re- warded to maintain a dynamic and successful contract system.

Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals and allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to their interests and needs.
This empowers students, fosters motivation, and facilitates mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. ~KA NOTES ON HONORS CONTRACTS KARL ASPELUND, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, URI HONORS OCTOBER 23, 2023

WHAT IS AN HONORS CONTRACT?
AN HONORS CONTRACT is a signed agreement between a student and in- structor.
Facilitated by the honors program, the contract states that the student will complete a specified project in addition to other coursework required and thus “convert” the non-honors class to an honors-equivalent course through additional work, such as outside reading, independent research, or some other enhanced learning activity (Badenhausen, 7).
Usually, students are required to earn both an A or B grade for the regular coursework and submit acceptable contract work to qualify for honors credit. (James, 30) A little over 60% of honors programs in the USA—regardless of institutional type—use contracts (Bahls, 172.) CONTRACTS provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough of a student body to fill hon- ors sections.
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth (Bahls, 175).

For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kan- sas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.
They can “facilitate access to honors, increase completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with struc- tured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences” (Dotter, 56).
Honors contracts not only maximize faculty-student contact in classes of any format, they also accommodate exploration and questioning in a range of research disciplines, from team-taught humanities discussions to innovative in- vestigations in STEM courses, including their labs (Myers and Whitebread, 22.) Further, as a valued part of honors education, tutorial-based contracts can be seen as a special approach used in various modes of learning: Research and creative scholarship, breadth and enduring questions, service learning and leadership, experiential learning, and learning communities.

They can therefore similarly result in the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learner-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors educa- tion (Myers and Whitebread, 40 & NCHC Shared Principles and Practices).
WHY USE HONORS CONTRACTS?
Provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility Empower students to their own learning experiences Maximize faculty-student contact Result in broader, deeper, and more complex learning centered and learner direct- ed experiences An agreement, mediated by the honors program, be- tween student and instructor that defines further work that“converts” the non-hon- ors class to an honors equivalent course. 60+ % of programs use contracts 2 Honors education is characterized by in-class and extracurricular activities that are measurably broader, deeper, or more complex than comparable learn - ing experiences typically found at institutions of higher education.

Honors expe - riences include a distinctive learner-directed environment and philosophy, pro - vide opportunities that are appropriately tailored to fit the institution’ s culture and mission, and frequently occur within a close community of students and faculty. ~National Collegiate Honors Council: Definition of Honors Education

HOW ARE CONTRACTS SET UP EFFECTIVELY?
A COMPREHENSIVE SET OF GUIDELINES, that include the basic expecta- tions of the honors experience and specific expectations for contracting, should be available and presented to students early on.
These should include that two of the primary purposes of contracting are to: 1) enable a student and faculty member to establish a one-to-one, ongoing mentor-mentee relationship through- out the semester and 2) to enable the student to experience the subject matter in more depth. (Bolsch, 54) Three honors-related dissertations reporting mixed experiences with contracts find or imply that students appreciate contracts when they meet two conditions: 1) student and faculty customize the work to fit a student’s interests, and 2) con- tracts involve significant time with the instructor (Myers and Whitebread: 23) Faculty members should be solely responsible for assigning course grades.
However, the contracting process should be structured from the outset as one in which the honors organization certifies that a successfully contracted course should be designated for “honors credit” on a student’s transcript.

So, while the faculty member assigns the grade for the course based on requirements unrelat- ed to the contract, honors administration is responsible for placing, essentially, a “seal of approval” on each contract experience through an additional transcript notation once it receives the faculty member’s certification that the elements of the contract were completed. (See: Bolsch, 52) Creating databases for honors advisors of all past digital contracts, searchable by course and faculty mentor’s name can lead to more proactive advising about innovative approaches to contracts and increased access to examples before students even meet with faculty. (Thomas & Hunter, 242) THE A V AILABILITY AND BENEFITS OF CONTRACTS need to be careful- ly publicized to newly-arrived honors students.
Honors advisors should initially help students understand where in their trajec- tory an honors contract might be instrumental and beneficial.
It should be made clear how important a dialogue with instructors will be, and how much this relies on student initiative and their own vision for their learning.

Honors administration and advisors should promote that students, immediate- ly on identifying a course within which they´d be interested to do contracted work, that they talk with an honors advisor to ensure that they understand the process and are aware of their options. “These meetings allow students to re- hearse future conversations with faculty in a safe environment, enable advisors to set clear expectations for contracts, and equip students with the necessary language to meet those expectations” (Dotter, 59.) Students should approach instructors before registering to discuss options and get a firm commitment so the contract is viable and that the honors credits they are receiving that term will be sufficient for their continuing success.
HOW SHOULD STUDENTS APPROACH SETTING UP A CONTRACT?
Searchable databases of past digital contracts lead to more proactive advising Publicize contracts early and often!
Encourage students to ap- proach advisors as soon as they see an opportunity for a contract arise.

Students must approach faculty—with the help of ad- vising— before registering to begin the process Two primary purposes: Enabling a mentor-mentee relationship and a more in-depth experience of the subject matter Students appreciate con- tracts that are fitted to their interests and afford signifi- cant time with the instructor Faculty assign grades, the honors organization ap- proves the honors credits and notifies Enrollment Services.
Advise students early on about the process and bene- fits of contracts 3
WHAT MIGHT A CONTRACT STIPULATE?

FIVE COMPONENTS should be, at least, required for a contract: 1) A substantial (15-20 p.) paper or project (of equivalent time/effort: c. 20 hours) should be defined and outlined. 2) It should be required that the student share the knowledge/skills/experienc- es gained through the paper or project with an audience, either in the class or elsewhere. 3) The contract should include a plan for how the faculty member and student have regular contact outside of class to discuss the student’s progress and an- swer questions regarding the paper or project. 4)The student should be required to state specifically on the contract form how they will meet each of the three NCHC requirements of “broader, deeper, more complex.” 5) A date at the midpoint of the semester should be determined at which the faculty member should provide a brief report to honors administration on the contact they have had with the student and assess the student’s progress to date. (See: Bolsch 2005: 55) CONTRACTS EXEMPLIFY THE BEST OF HONORS PEDAGOGY when, anchored in the tutorial model, they cultivate personalized, mentored learning and ensure consistent, documented quality (Myers and Whitebread, 22).
